title: Tax the Super-Rich to Save Lives, Says Report
paragraphs: As many countries cut funding for international development, wealth distribution policies like taxing the super-rich could prevent millions of deaths by 2030.

This is what a study published in The Lancet has found. Researchers from the Barcelona Institute for Global Health first analyzed data from 59 low-income countries between 2002 and 2021, and used this to project future scenarios.
In particular, the researchers examined the relationship between death rates and development assistance from wealthier countries.
They found that higher levels of development assistance were linked with a 24% reduction in overall deaths, as well as a 33% reduction in deaths among children under 5.

However, many wealthy countries have recently cut their development assistance to other nations. In 2023, France, Germany, Japan, the UK and the US accounted for around 70% of the over $250 billion spent on development around the world — but in 2024 and 2025, each of these countries reduced their spending.
If this level of defunding continues through to 2030, the researchers estimate it could lead to 7.6 million additional deaths, including 1.4 million more children.
The researchers then looked at 10 wealth distribution policies that have been considered in recent high-level international discussions.

These included increased taxes on a number of things, such as billionaires, international corporations, certain financial transactions, carbon emissions, cryptocurrencies, and interest earned by creditors that loan poorer nations money.
The study calculated how the money raised by these policies could make up for shortfalls in international development funding.
It found that, even at moderate tax rates, each policy could generate enough money to offset part, or even all, of the projected negative health impacts associated with reduced international aid.
For example, a 3% wealth tax on billionaires was associated with preventing 30 million deaths by 2030, while even a 1% billionaire tax could save 15 million lives.

The researchers also estimated that relatively low taxes on large foreign exchange transactions could result in 25 million fewer deaths, while a global minimum tax on large multinational corporations could prevent up to 20 million.
